RULE E-ANS (an answer to a pressed verse). Decide FIRST what the right grade is: MEETS only when the answer shows, in its own words, how the verse fits the answering side's case, or why the stated meaning does not follow from what the verse says. MISSES when the answer rests on an absence (it says only that the verse, or the other side, names no, states no, does not name, gives no, or is silent on something) without a fit of its own, or when it does not address the stated meaning. An answer that quotes the verse's own words against the specific claim of the stated meaning (for example, the verse's own stated grounds set against a claim that there were no grounds) shows why the meaning does not follow: it MEETS, even when it closes with a bare assertion such as "It fits the link". Then for each judge's grade: AGREE when it matches the right grade, DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-VOID (a listed premise ruled VOID). A premise is VOID only when its charge says the opponent's quoted words state something they do not state (a negation, a universal, or another claim beyond the quote). The charge is the premise's own words before its quote (for example "The inference that ..."), read against the words of that quote. Set aside only a clause saying what the premise props ("which props ...") or a sentence naming the objection it serves ("The objection it props is ..."); those are not part of the charge. AGREE with the VOID ruling when the charge goes beyond its quote; DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-COL (a collision line: FORCED, or LINK BROKEN). A link is broken only when the answer's own quoted words cannot agree with the meaning pressed, as the line quotes them; it is not broken because no verse states it, or because of an absence, and it is not broken by a rival reading: an answer that reads a contested word another way, with its own layers quoted in its round, can agree with the meaning on its own reading (pkgECF, W3 2534; either side alike). A link is also broken when a proven press against it was left unanswered (Commitment 5) and the line quotes the pressing sentence and names its round (ruling 392); that is not a break by absence. When the item says the FAILS words are found exactly in the round of the answer, those words are the answering side's own and are read as part of its answer. AGREE when the quoted words show the answer cannot agree with the meaning; DISAGREE when they do carry a meaning the link can agree with, or the line rests on an absence or on a demand for a stating verse. A line's layers after GROUND ([L1], [L2], [L3]; Commitment 13) are counted in code, not by you: read them as the judge's grounds.
RULE E-SYN (a sentence of the synthesis saying a side withdrew, conceded, granted, dropped or narrowed something). AGREE when that side's own sentences given you give up that same thing at the same scope; DISAGREE when they do not, or give up less (for example, "no row I cite" is not "no biblical text").
RULE E-HOLD (a collision line graded STANDS or UNDERDETERMINED). STANDS is right only when the answering side's own words, as quoted to you in the line or in this judge's ANSWER CHECK lines, carry a meaning the link can agree with for the meaning pressed. UNDERDETERMINED is right only when the quoted words show that both readings agree with the pressed verse and neither side's words show that the other cannot. BROKEN when the answer's quoted words cannot agree with the meaning pressed, or the answer is only a bare grant or an absence with no fit of its own. A ground that rests on an absence (no verse states it, the text does not narrate it), or on the judge's own reading rather than the debate's words, is not a ground. Each ANSWER CHECK line given you is labelled with whose answer it grades: a MISSES or FAILS on the challenger's answer counts against the challenger's link, never against the defender's, and the reverse. A press labelled UNPROVEN carries no answering burden, so a MISSES on it breaks nothing. For a link-state line ("D5: STANDS"), the quoted answers are that side's ANSWER CHECK lines given you: STANDS is right unless one of them, on a press against this link, is MISSES or FAILS. AGREE when the judge's grade is right; DISAGREE when it is not.
RULE E-KEY (the keystone line). The keystone grade must follow from this judge's own collision lines on that link, given to you: STANDS only when none of them grades the link BROKEN or FORCED and the link was not withdrawn; BROKEN when one of them does. Its ground, where it gives one, must rest on the debate's words, not on the judge's own statement of doctrine. AGREE when the keystone grade follows and its ground rests on the debate's words; DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-PREM (a listed premise, and how each judge ruled it). The judges' own rules, quoted: "A LINK ROUND answer that neither exhibits the premise's layer footing nor concedes counts as CONCEDED." "SELF-SUPPORTED = every listed defender claim is carried by its layer stack -- each [L4] exhibits the [L1]/[L2]/[L3] footing it rests on (at least two prior layers exhibited; a shown chain counts equally)." For a charge in the form ASSUMES: ... -- ROWS GIVE: ...: "the premise is UNEXHIBITED when no quoted row gives the fact it assumes, and it stands when a row the side quoted gives that fact." "UNEXHIBITED also fires ... when a narrowed link keeps words that still assert what its own side gave up." And: "What a link INFERS from its rows is its [L4]: it is graded by the two-layer rule and by the meaning of the verses pressed against it, and never as a missing row (DG-61); an inferred act, such as a begetting or a knowing, is never an ASSUMES." A premise "charged in terms stronger than its quote, is VOID" (RULE E-VOID). For premise N only, decide FIRST the right ruling: COUNTED (UNEXHIBITED or CONCEDED), SPARED, or VOID. The judges' form reads "Itemize the counted links": a premise the judge's line does not name is that judge's SPARED ruling. AGREE when the judge's ruling on premise N (named, or spared by silence) is the right one; DISAGREE when it is not; NO ANSWER only when the judge's line is not in its form. A NARROWED premise (the side drops a claim and keeps the link on a narrower footing, with its [L1] and [L2] or [L3] exhibited) is SPARED: dropping a claim is not conceding the premise, and the dropped claim alone never makes the premise COUNTED. It is UNEXHIBITED only when the kept words still assert the very claim the side dropped; say so by quoting both the dropped claim and the kept words that still assert it.
RULE E-RES (a judge's RESULT line). Its arithmetic is checked in code. Read only its reason sentence: by the judges' Commitment 1 (the record is the only evidence) and Commitment 3 (ruling 405), a reason that rests on an absence (no verse states it, the text does not narrate it) or on the judge's own doctrine rather than the debate's words is not a reason. FOLLOWS when the reason rests on the debate's words; DOES NOT FOLLOW when it does not, quoting the words that show it. AGREE when FOLLOWS; DISAGREE when DOES NOT FOLLOW.
NO ANSWER, for every rule: the judge's line lacks its grade or its ground, or is not in its form. It reports a violation by the judge; it is never your own uncertainty, and you choose AGREE or DISAGREE whenever the line can be read.
Reply with exactly one line per judge id, and nothing else, in this form:

RULE E-ANS (an answer to a pressed verse). Decide FIRST what the right grade is: MEETS only when the answer shows, in its own words, how the verse fits the answering side's case, or why the stated meaning does not follow from what the verse says. MISSES when the answer rests on an absence (it says only that the verse, or the other side, names no, states no, does not name, gives no, or is silent on something) without a fit of its own, or when it does not address the stated meaning. An answer that quotes the verse's own words against the specific claim of the stated meaning (for example, the verse's own stated grounds set against a claim that there were no grounds) shows why the meaning does not follow: it MEETS, even when it closes with a bare assertion such as "It fits the link". Then for each judge's grade: AGREE when it matches the right grade, DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-VOID (a listed premise ruled VOID). A premise is VOID only when its charge says the opponent's quoted words state something they do not state (a negation, a universal, or another claim beyond the quote). The charge is the premise's own words before its quote (for example "The inference that ..."), read against the words of that quote. Set aside only a clause saying what the premise props ("which props ...") or a sentence naming the objection it serves ("The objection it props is ..."); those are not part of the charge. AGREE with the VOID ruling when the charge goes beyond its quote; DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-COL (a collision line: FORCED, or LINK BROKEN). A link is broken only when the answer's own quoted words cannot agree with the meaning pressed, as the line quotes them; it is not broken because no verse states it, or because of an absence, and it is not broken by a rival reading: an answer that reads a contested word another way, with its own layers quoted in its round, can agree with the meaning on its own reading (pkgECF, W3 2534; either side alike). A link is also broken when a proven press against it was left unanswered (Commitment 5) and the line quotes the pressing sentence and names its round (ruling 392); that is not a break by absence. When the item says the FAILS words are found exactly in the round of the answer, those words are the answering side's own and are read as part of its answer. AGREE when the quoted words show the answer cannot agree with the meaning; DISAGREE when they do carry a meaning the link can agree with, or the line rests on an absence or on a demand for a stating verse. A line's layers after GROUND ([L1], [L2], [L3]; Commitment 13) are counted in code, not by you: read them as the judge's grounds.
RULE E-SYN (a sentence of the synthesis saying a side withdrew, conceded, granted, dropped or narrowed something). AGREE when that side's own sentences given you give up that same thing at the same scope; DISAGREE when they do not, or give up less (for example, "no row I cite" is not "no biblical text").
RULE E-HOLD (a collision line graded STANDS or UNDERDETERMINED). STANDS is right only when the answering side's own words, as quoted to you in the line or in this judge's ANSWER CHECK lines, carry a meaning the link can agree with for the meaning pressed. UNDERDETERMINED is right only when the quoted words show that both readings agree with the pressed verse and neither side's words show that the other cannot. BROKEN when the answer's quoted words cannot agree with the meaning pressed, or the answer is only a bare grant or an absence with no fit of its own. A ground that rests on an absence (no verse states it, the text does not narrate it), or on the judge's own reading rather than the debate's words, is not a ground. Each ANSWER CHECK line given you is labelled with whose answer it grades: a MISSES or FAILS on the challenger's answer counts against the challenger's link, never against the defender's, and the reverse. A press labelled UNPROVEN carries no answering burden, so a MISSES on it breaks nothing. For a link-state line ("D5: STANDS"), the quoted answers are that side's ANSWER CHECK lines given you: STANDS is right unless one of them, on a press against this link, is MISSES or FAILS. AGREE when the judge's grade is right; DISAGREE when it is not.
RULE E-KEY (the keystone line). The keystone grade must follow from this judge's own collision lines on that link, given to you: STANDS only when none of them grades the link BROKEN or FORCED and the link was not withdrawn; BROKEN when one of them does. Its ground, where it gives one, must rest on the debate's words, not on the judge's own statement of doctrine. AGREE when the keystone grade follows and its ground rests on the debate's words; DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-PREM (a listed premise, and how each judge ruled it). The judges' own rules, quoted: "A LINK ROUND answer that neither exhibits the premise's layer footing nor concedes counts as CONCEDED." "SELF-SUPPORTED = every listed defender claim is carried by its layer stack -- each [L4] exhibits the [L1]/[L2]/[L3] footing it rests on (at least two prior layers exhibited; a shown chain counts equally)." For a charge in the form ASSUMES: ... -- ROWS GIVE: ...: "the premise is UNEXHIBITED when no quoted row gives the fact it assumes, and it stands when a row the side quoted gives that fact." "UNEXHIBITED also fires ... when a narrowed link keeps words that still assert what its own side gave up." RULE E-ANS (an answer to a pressed verse). Decide FIRST what the right grade is: MEETS only when the answer shows, in its own words, how the verse fits the answering side's case, or why the stated meaning does not follow from what the verse says. MISSES when the answer rests on an absence (it says only that the verse, or the other side, names no, states no, does not name, gives no, or is silent on something) without a fit of its own, or when it does not address the stated meaning. An answer that quotes the verse's own words against the specific claim of the stated meaning (for example, the verse's own stated grounds set against a claim that there were no grounds) shows why the meaning does not follow: it MEETS, even when it closes with a bare assertion such as "It fits the link". Then for each judge's grade: AGREE when it matches the right grade, DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-VOID (a listed premise ruled VOID). A premise is VOID only when its charge says the opponent's quoted words state something they do not state (a negation, a universal, or another claim beyond the quote). The charge is the premise's own words before its quote (for example "The inference that ..."), read against the words of that quote. Set aside only a clause saying what the premise props ("which props ...") or a sentence naming the objection it serves ("The objection it props is ..."); those are not part of the charge. AGREE with the VOID ruling when the charge goes beyond its quote; DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-COL (a collision line: FORCED, or LINK BROKEN). A link is broken only when the answer's own quoted words cannot agree with the meaning pressed, as the line quotes them; it is not broken because no verse states it, or because of an absence, and it is not broken by a rival reading: an answer that reads a contested word another way, with its own layers quoted in its round, can agree with the meaning on its own reading (pkgECF, W3 2534; either side alike). A link is also broken when a proven press against it was left unanswered (Commitment 5) and the line quotes the pressing sentence and names its round (ruling 392); that is not a break by absence. AGREE when the quoted words show the answer cannot agree with the meaning; DISAGREE when they do carry a meaning the link can agree with, or the line rests on an absence or on a demand for a stating verse. RULE E-SYN (a sentence of the synthesis saying a side withdrew, conceded, granted, dropped or narrowed something). RULE E-HOLD (a collision line graded STANDS or UNDERDETERMINED). STANDS is right only when the answering side's own words, as quoted to you in the line or in this judge's ANSWER CHECK lines, carry a meaning the link can agree with for the meaning pressed. UNDERDETERMINED is right only when the quoted words show that both readings agree with the pressed verse and neither side's words show that the other cannot. BROKEN when the answer's quoted words cannot agree with the meaning pressed, or the answer is only a bare grant or an absence with no fit of its own. A ground that rests on an absence (no verse states it, the text does not narrate it), or on the judge's own reading rather than the debate's words, is not a ground. RULE E-ANS (an answer to a pressed verse). Decide FIRST what the right grade is: MEETS only when the answer shows, in its own words, how the verse fits the answering side's case, or why the stated meaning does not follow from what the verse says. MISSES when the answer rests on an absence (it says only that the verse, or the other side, names no, states no, does not name, gives no, or is silent on something) without a fit of its own, or when it does not address the stated meaning. An answer that quotes the verse's own words against the specific claim of the stated meaning (for example, the verse's own stated grounds set against a claim that there were no grounds) shows why the meaning does not follow: it MEETS, even when it closes with a bare assertion such as "It fits the link". Then for each judge's grade: AGREE when it matches the right grade, DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-VOID (a listed premise ruled VOID). A premise is VOID only when its charge says the opponent's quoted words state something they do not state (a negation, a universal, or another claim beyond the quote). The charge is the premise's own words before its quote (for example "The inference that ..."), read against the words of that quote. Set aside only a clause saying what the premise props ("which props ...") or a sentence naming the objection it serves ("The objection it props is ..."); those are not part of the charge. AGREE with the VOID ruling when the charge goes beyond its quote; DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-COL (a collision line: FORCED, or LINK BROKEN). A link is broken only when the answer's own quoted words cannot agree with the meaning pressed, as the line quotes them; it is not broken because no verse states it, or because of an absence, and it is not broken by a rival reading: an answer that reads a contested word another way, with its own layers quoted in its round, can agree with the meaning on its own reading (pkgECF, W3 2534; either side alike). A link is also broken when a proven press against it was left unanswered (Commitment 5) and the line quotes the pressing sentence and names its round (ruling 392); that is not a break by absence. When the item says the FAILS words are found exactly in the round of the answer, those words are the answering side's own and are read as part of its answer. AGREE when the quoted words show the answer cannot agree with the meaning; DISAGREE when they do carry a meaning the link can agree with, or the line rests on an absence or on a demand for a stating verse. A line's layers after GROUND ([L1], [L2], [L3]; Commitment 13) are counted in code, not by you: read them as the judge's grounds.
RULE E-SYN (a sentence of the synthesis saying a side withdrew, conceded, granted, dropped or narrowed something). AGREE when that side's own sentences given you give up that same thing at the same scope; DISAGREE when they do not, or give up less (for example, "no row I cite" is not "no biblical text").
RULE E-HOLD (a collision line graded STANDS or UNDERDETERMINED). STANDS is right only when the answering side's own words, as quoted to you in the line or in this judge's ANSWER CHECK lines, carry a meaning the link can agree with for the meaning pressed. UNDERDETERMINED is right only when the quoted words show that both readings agree with the pressed verse and neither side's words show that the other cannot. BROKEN when the answer's quoted words cannot agree with the meaning pressed, or the answer is only a bare grant or an absence with no fit of its own. A ground that rests on an absence (no verse states it, the text does not narrate it), or on the judge's own reading rather than the debate's words, is not a ground. Each ANSWER CHECK line given you is labelled with whose answer it grades: a MISSES or FAILS on the challenger's answer counts against the challenger's link, never against the defender's, and the reverse. A press labelled UNPROVEN carries no answering burden, so a MISSES on it breaks nothing. For a link-state line ("D5: STANDS"), the quoted answers are that side's ANSWER CHECK lines given you: STANDS is right unless one of them, on a press against this link, is MISSES or FAILS. AGREE when the judge's grade is right; DISAGREE when it is not.
RULE E-KEY (the keystone line). The keystone grade must follow from this judge's own collision lines on that link, given to you: STANDS only when none of them grades the link BROKEN or FORCED and the link was not withdrawn; BROKEN when one of them does. Its ground, where it gives one, must rest on the debate's words, not on the judge's own statement of doctrine. AGREE when the keystone grade follows and its ground rests on the debate's words; DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-PREM (a listed premise, and how each judge ruled it). The judges' own rules, quoted: "A LINK ROUND answer that neither exhibits the premise's layer footing nor concedes counts as CONCEDED." "SELF-SUPPORTED = every listed defender claim is carried by its layer stack -- each [L4] exhibits the [L1]/[L2]/[L3] footing it rests on (at least two prior layers exhibited; a shown chain counts equally)." For a charge in the form ASSUMES: ... -- ROWS GIVE: ...: "the premise is UNEXHIBITED when no quoted row gives the fact it assumes, and it stands when a row the side quoted gives that fact." "UNEXHIBITED also fires ... when a narrowed link keeps words that still assert what its own side gave up." And: "What a link INFERS from its rows is its [L4]: it is graded by the two-layer rule and by the meaning of the verses pressed against it, and never as a missing row (DG-61); an inferred act, such as a begetting or a knowing, is never an ASSUMES." A premise "charged in terms stronger than its quote, is VOID" (RULE E-VOID). For premise N only, decide FIRST the right ruling: COUNTED (UNEXHIBITED or CONCEDED), SPARED, or VOID. The judges' form reads "Itemize the counted links": a premise the judge's line does not name is that judge's SPARED ruling. AGREE when the judge's ruling on premise N (named, or spared by silence) is the right one; DISAGREE when it is not; NO ANSWER only when the judge's line is not in its form. RULE E-ANS (an answer to a pressed verse). Decide FIRST what the right grade is: MEETS only when the answer shows, in its own words, how the verse fits the answering side's case, or why the stated meaning does not follow from what the verse says. MISSES when the answer rests on an absence (it says only that the verse, or the other side, names no, states no, does not name, gives no, or is silent on something) without a fit of its own, or when it does not address the stated meaning. An answer that quotes the verse's own words against the specific claim of the stated meaning (for example, the verse's own stated grounds set against a claim that there were no grounds) shows why the meaning does not follow: it MEETS, even when it closes with a bare assertion such as "It fits the link". Then for each judge's grade: AGREE when it matches the right grade, DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-VOID (a listed premise ruled VOID). A premise is VOID only when its charge says the opponent's quoted words state something they do not state (a negation, a universal, or another claim beyond the quote). The charge is the premise's own words before its quote (for example "The inference that ..."), read against the words of that quote. Set aside only a clause saying what the premise props ("which props ...") or a sentence naming the objection it serves ("The objection it props is ..."); those are not part of the charge. AGREE with the VOID ruling when the charge goes beyond its quote; DISAGREE when it does not.
RULE E-COL (a collision line: FORCED, or LINK BROKEN). A link is broken only when the answer's own quoted words cannot agree with the meaning pressed, as the line quotes them; it is not broken because no verse states it, or because of an absence, and it is not broken by a rival reading: an answer that reads a contested word another way, with its own layers quoted in its round, can agree with the meaning on its own reading (pkgECF, W3 2534; either side alike). A link is also broken when a proven press against it was left unanswered (Commitment 5) and the line quotes the pressing sentence and names its round (ruling 392); that is not a break by absence. When the item says the FAILS words are found exactly in the round of the answer, those words are the answering side's own and are read as part of its answer. AGREE when the quoted words show the answer cannot agree with the meaning; DISAGREE when they do carry a meaning the link can agree with, or the line rests on an absence or on a demand for a stating verse. DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening Case: Christ Had No Human Biological Father

**Position.** By "biological father" I mean a human male who contributed to the conception. The KJV text says that Jesus Christ was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, while she was a virgin, and that Joseph was only his supposed father. [L4, resting on the layered points below]

---

## 1. The genealogy breaks at Joseph

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2 uses the unbroken pattern of begetting: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren". Matthew 1:16 then departs from it: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** The verb in both verses is *gennaō* (G1080), meaning "to beget" when a man is its subject and "to be born" when passive. In 1:16 the verb is passive, *egennēthē*, "was born". The relative pronoun is *ex hēs* (ἐξ ἧς), "out of whom", and it is feminine singular. Grammatically it can refer only to Mary. It cannot refer to Joseph, or to Joseph and Mary together.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20 confirms where the weight falls: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost". The source of the conception is named as the Holy Ghost, not Joseph.

**[L4]** Matthew keeps "begat" for every man in the list. For Jesus alone he changes to a passive verb and a feminine pronoun. The text therefore withholds the father-begetting formula from the one birth it narrates in the next verses. This rests on the Greek grammar of 1:16 [L2] and the contrast with 1:2 [L1/L3].

---

## 2. The conception was "of the Holy Ghost" before Joseph and Mary came together

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** The phrase is *ek pneumatos hagiou* (ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου), "out of the Spirit, holy", which names the source. The verb *synelthein* (G4905) means "to come together". The conception is placed before that coming together.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** In Luke 1:35, *episkiazō* (G1982) means "to overshadow". *Dio kai* means "therefore also", a causal link. The title "Son of God" follows from this conception.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 gives the timing and Luke 1:35 gives the cause. Together they give a conception with a divine source and without a prior human act. Both are named in the text, and no human male is named as a contributor.

---

## 3. Mary was a virgin and Joseph did not know her

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son".

**[L2]** In Luke 1:34, *ginōskō* (G1097) means "to know", used of sexual relations, and *andra* (G435) means "a man", a male person. In Matthew 1:25, *eginōsken* (ἐγίνωσκεν) is the same verb, imperfect, "was not knowing her". *Heōs hou* means "until".

**[L3]** Matthew 1:23 quotes the prophecy: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son". Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** In Isaiah 7:14 the word behind the KJV's "virgin" is *almah* (H5959). In Matthew 1:23 the word is *parthenos* (G3933), "virgin". Genesis 24:43 uses *almah* for Rebekah: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw water". Genesis 24:16 describes her as "a virgin, neither had any man known her".

**[L4]** The KJV's own usage of the word behind Isaiah 7:14 includes a woman defined as never known by a man (Genesis 24:16, 24:43). Matthew 1:23 applies the prophecy to Mary with *parthenos*. Mary's own words in Luke 1:34 and the statement of Matthew 1:25 exclude a prior union with Joseph or any man.

---

## 4. Joseph was the supposed father, not the begetter

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (ἐνομίζετο, G3543) means "was thought, was reckoned by custom". It marks a belief held by others, not a statement of fact by the narrator.

**[L3]** John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" This is what the crowd says, not what the narrator says. Luke 2:48–49 sets two fathers side by side. Mary says, "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing". The child answers, "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Matthew 1:19 shows Joseph's own reaction: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L4]** Joseph's intent to put Mary away shows he knew he was not the father (Matthew 1:19 [L1]). The angel's words tell him to "take unto thee Mary thy wife" because the conception is "of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:20 [L3]). The title "father" in the mouths of Mary and the crowd (Luke 2:48; John 6:42) is a social and legal title. Luke 3:23 marks it as supposition (*enomizeto* [L2]).

---

## 5. "Made of a woman" and the seed of the woman

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law".

**[L2]** *Genomenon ek gynaikos* (γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός) means "come to be out of a woman". Only the woman is named as the human source.

**[L3]** Genesis 3:15: "I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed". *Zera* (H2233) means "seed", and here it is "her seed", a seed attributed to the woman. John 1:14: "the Word was made flesh". Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me".

**[L4]** The KJV names a woman's seed in Genesis 3:15 and a birth "of a woman" in Galatians 4:4, with no human male named. Hebrews 10:5 says the body was prepared by God. The footing is [L1] Galatians 4:4 and [L3] Genesis 3:15.

---

## Anticipating the press: "seed of David"

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh". Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David".

**[L2]** *Sperma* (G4690) means "seed, offspring, descendant". In Romans 1:3, *genomenou* ("made") is the same verb family as in Galatians 4:4, and it is tied to descent, not to a male parent.

**[L3]** In Matthew 1:16 the birth is "of whom", feminine. Luke 1:27 names Mary as "a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David". "Father David" is used in the sense of ancestor, as "father Abraham" is used elsewhere.

**[L4]** The Davidic descent is stated "according to the flesh" and is carried by the woman, since the birth is "of her" (Matthew 1:16 [L2]). The text does not say that Joseph's seed produced the child, and Joseph is placed in the line by legal adoption into the house (Matthew 1:20 [L1], "take unto thee"). This is held as an [L4] on two footings, Romans 1:3 with Galatians 4:4 and Matthew 1:16 with the feminine pronoun, not as a bare claim.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on:

1. Matthew's genealogy breaks the "begat" pattern at Joseph and assigns Jesus' birth to Mary alone. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:2 ("Abraham begat Isaac") against Matthew 1:16 ("of whom was born Jesus"); [L2] *ex hēs* (ἐξ ἧς), "out of whom", feminine singular, with *gennaō* passive.
2. The conception was "of the Holy Ghost" and occurred before Joseph and Mary came together. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18 ("before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost"); [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Spirit, holy"; [L3] Luke 1:35 ("The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God").
3. Mary was a virgin and Joseph did not know her until after the birth. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34 ("seeing I know not a man") and Matthew 1:25 ("And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son"); [L2] *ginōskō* (G1097), "to know" in the sexual sense, and *parthenos* (G3933), "virgin"; [L3] Isaiah 7:14 ("Behold, a virgin shall conceive") with Genesis 24:16.
4. Joseph is called father only as "supposed" and by social custom. Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23 ("being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph"); [L2] *enomizeto* (G3543), "was thought, reckoned"; [L3] Matthew 1:19 and Luke 2:48–49.
5. Christ was "made of a woman" and is called the woman's seed, with no human male named. Footing: [L1] Galatians 4:4 ("made of a woman"); [L2] *genomenon ek gynaikos*, "come to be out of a woman"; [L3] Genesis 3:15 ("her seed").
6. Therefore Christ had no human biological father. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:20 ("that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost") with Luke 1:35; [L2] *gennēthen* (G1080), "conceived/begotten", in Matthew 1:20, with *ek pneumatos hagiou*, "out of the Spirit, holy"; [L3] Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:25.

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, RESPONSE

# Defender, Round 2: Answers to the Presses and the Link Round

Three points of discipline come first, so the judges can see what stands and what does not.

- **Genesis 24:16.** The challenger is right that Genesis 24:16 carries *bethulah* (H1330), not *almah* (H5959). I correct my wording below.
- **"Made of a woman."** Galatians 4:4 alone does not exclude a father, because Matthew 11:11 and Job 14:1 use the same phrase of men who had fathers. I keep D5 only as a cumulative witness.
- **Mary's descent.** No quoted row states that Mary was of David's house. I drop the sentence that said so.

None of these three carries the keystone. D6 stands on the source of the conception in Matthew 1:18, 1:20 and Luke 1:34-35.

---

## A. Answer to the press on D6 (the keystone)

**1. "Of the Holy Ghost" beside "son of David" (Matthew 1:20).**

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *Ek* (out of) names the source. *Gennaō* (G1080), "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother)", stands behind the margin's "begotten". *Phobeō* (G5399), "to be alarmed", names Joseph's fear.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:19: "was minded to put her away privily". Matthew 1:20 begins "But while he thought on these things" (*enthymeomai*, G1760, "ponder").

**[L4]** The angel answers Joseph's pondering with the words "fear not... for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost". A "for" that removes a fear states the source of the conception as the ground of reassurance. If Joseph's own act were the source, there would be nothing to fear and nothing to explain. The title "son of David" addresses him as heir of the house who is to take the child in. It does not say he begat it. The footings are Matthew 1:20 [L1] with *ek* [L2], and Matthew 1:19 [L3].

**2. John 1:13, 1 John 5:1 and 1 John 3:9.**

**[L1]** John 1:13: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."

**[L3]** 1 John 3:9: "Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin; for his seed remaineth in him". The "seed" there is spiritual and is kept in the believer. It is not a body formed at conception.

**[L4]** The verse excludes "blood", "the will of the flesh" and "the will of man" as the source of that birth. It puts "of God" in their place. The challenger reads the believers' birth as a second birth beside a fleshly father. That birth is an additional one that makes believers children of God. In Matthew 1:20 the same word *ek* names the only source of "that which is conceived in her". The two uses differ in what they describe, a rebirth in one and a conception in the other. They share only a preposition. Footings: John 1:13 [L1] with 1 John 3:9 [L3], and *ek* [L2].

**3. Luke 1:35, "therefore also".**

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* (therefore also) is a causal link. It follows the clause directly before it in the same verse, "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... overshadow thee". *Epi sou* and *ex sou* ("upon thee", "of thee") name Mary as the one acted on and the one born "of".

**[L3]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Luke 1:37: "For with God nothing shall be impossible." Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb".

**[L4]** Mary asks how a conception can occur when she knows "not a man". The angel's answer is that the Holy Ghost will come upon her. Luke 1:37 then closes the answer with the impossibility of nothing with God. If the answer were "by Joseph after the wedding", it would not answer her question, and Luke 1:37 would have nothing to meet. The title "Son of God" is stated as following "therefore" from the coming upon. It does not rest back on Luke 1:32 alone. Footings: Luke 1:35 [L1] with *dio kai* [L2], and Luke 1:34 and 1:37 [L3].

**4. Solomon (1 Chronicles 28:6; 2 Samuel 7:14).**

**[L1]** 1 Chronicles 28:6: "for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."

**[L3]** Luke 1:35: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God".

**[L4]** Solomon's sonship is by "I have chosen him". Luke 1:35 gives a cause in the birth itself: "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born". The two grounds differ. The verse attaches the title to the conception, and Solomon's verse attaches it to a choice. Footings: 1 Chronicles 28:6 [L1] against Luke 1:35 [L3].

**5. Acts 1:8, Luke 9:34, Acts 5:15.**

**[L1]** Acts 1:8: "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you". Luke 9:34: "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them".

**[L2]** *Eperchomai* (to come upon) and *episkiazō* (G1982, to overshadow) name presence and power. The effect each verb has is given by its own context.

**[L3]** In Acts 1:8 the effect is "ye shall be witnesses unto me". In Luke 1:35 the effect clause is "that holy thing which shall be born of thee", with Luke 1:31 "thou shalt conceive in thy womb" before it.

**[L4]** The verbs are the same, and each context supplies its result. In Acts 1:8 the result is witness. In Luke 1:35, in answer to the question of Luke 1:34, the result is a birth. The challenger's argument assumes the verb alone sets the result. The footings show the context sets it. Footings: Acts 1:8 [L1], *eperchomai* [L2], Luke 1:31 [L3].

## B. Answer to the press on D1

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** *Egennēsen* (begat) governs "Joseph" as its object. Jacob is the begetter and Joseph is the one begotten. *Egennēthē* (was born) is passive and takes *ex hēs* (out of whom), feminine singular. The verb of begetting never takes Joseph as its subject in this clause.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob". 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels". Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ".

**[L4]** The clause names the husband and still gives the begetting no man as subject. The rest of the chain is "begat... begat... begat", and this clause is the one place it turns to "was born" with a feminine relative. Joseph is named as husband, which is the status Matthew 1:19 gives him. The promises of 2 Samuel 7:12 and Acts 2:30 name David's loins as the origin of the line. They do not name Joseph's loins as the last step, and a genealogy can pass through a husband by legal reckoning, as I show in section F. Footings: Matthew 1:16 [L1] with *ex hēs* [L2], Matthew 1:2 [L3].

## C. Answer to the press on D2

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *Mnēsteuō* (G3423), "to betroth", gives the status. *Synerchomai* names the coming together, which is the home-taking. *Heurethē* ("she was found") is passive and names a discovery.

**[L3]** Deuteronomy 22:24: "because he hath humbled his neighbour's wife". Matthew 1:24: "took unto him his wife". Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son".

**[L4]** I grant that the betrothed was already a wife in law (Deuteronomy 22:24), and that Joseph is "her husband" in Matthew 1:19. That grants a status and not an act. Matthew 1:18 says "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost". The source is stated as the Holy Ghost at the time she is found. Matthew 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not" until the birth, and that statement is made of the very marriage the challenger says Joseph used. Footings: Matthew 1:18 [L1] with *heurethē* [L2], and Matthew 1:25 and Deuteronomy 22:24 [L3].

## D. Answer to the press on D3 and Isaiah 7:14

**Luke 1:34.**

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* (to know) in the present tense gives her condition when she spoke. *Anēr* (G435), "a man (properly as an individual male)", names any man. It is not limited to a particular man.

**[L3]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph... and the virgin's name [was] Mary." Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb".

**[L4]** Mary is already espoused to Joseph (Luke 1:27). She is told she will conceive (Luke 1:31). She asks "How?", with "not a man". If the plan were conception in the marriage, she would know how. Her question treats the conception as one that dispenses with a man, and the answer in Luke 1:35 confirms it. Footings: Luke 1:34 [L1] with *anēr* [L2], Luke 1:27 and 1:31 [L3].

**Isaiah 7:14.**

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** I correct my wording. Genesis 24:16 uses *bethulah* (H1330), "virgin". Genesis 24:43 uses *almah* (H5959), which the KJV renders "virgin", for the same Rebekah of Genesis 24:16. In the KJV's own text the word behind Isaiah 7:14 is applied to a woman the same chapter says "neither had any man known her".

**[L3]** Genesis 24:43: "when the virgin cometh forth to draw [water]". Genesis 24:16: "a virgin, neither had any man known her". Isaiah 7:11: "Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above."

**[L4]** The challenger's set is Proverbs 30:19 ("a man with a maid"), Isaiah 7:16 and Isaiah 8:3. Proverbs 30:19 shows the KJV also renders *almah* "maid". The sign is a sign "of the LORD", asked "in the depth, or in the height", which is the language of a wonder. A conception by ordinary approach is no sign. Isaiah 8:3 differs on three points: the child is "Mahershalalhashbaz" and not "Immanuel", the woman is "the prophetess", and the child is the prophet's own. Matthew 1:22-23 states its own fulfilment: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child", with *parthenos* (G3933), "virgin". Luke 1:27 calls Mary by the same word. Footings: Isaiah 7:14 [L1] with *almah* [L2], Genesis 24:16 and 24:43 [L3].

## E. Answer to the press on D4

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli".

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (G3543), "was thought, was reckoned by custom". I grant the challenger's point from Acts 16:13 ("wont to be made") that the word carries a sense of custom. Luke 3:23 places it in parentheses before "the son of Joseph", so it qualifies that sonship as held by others.

**[L3]** Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled". Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing". Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

**[L4]** The same writer who gives Mary's words at Luke 2:48 writes "as was supposed" at Luke 3:23, after Luke 1:34-35. He names Joseph without the word "father" in his own narration at Luke 2:33. The reply at Luke 2:49 sets "my Father's" against "thy father". The word "parents" (Luke 2:27, 2:41) is a household term and not a verdict on begetting. Footings: Luke 3:23 [L1] with *enomizeto* [L2], Luke 2:33 and 2:49 [L3].

## F. The challenger's question: Hebrews 7:14 and the fathers' house

**[L1]** Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda".

**[L2]** *Anatellō* (G393), "to spring up, to arise", is said of the tribe. It does not say through whom.

**[L3]** The KJV shows reckoning of a man by a house that is not his begetter's:
- Genesis 48:5: "Ephraim and Manasseh... are mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine."
- Ruth 4:17: "There is a son born to Naomi".
- Ezra 2:61: "which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name".
- Matthew 1:21: "thou shalt call his name JESUS". Matthew 1:25: "and he called his name JESUS". Matthew 1:20: "take unto thee Mary thy wife".

**[L4]** The law of the fathers' house (Numbers 1:2) registered a man by the house that named him. Jacob's grandsons were counted as sons (Genesis 48:5). A son born to Naomi was counted hers (Ruth 4:17). A man could be called by his wife's father's name (Ezra 2:61). Joseph is told to take Mary and to name the child (Matthew 1:20-21), and Matthew 1:25 says he did name him. That is the act by which the child enters his house. I withdraw the word "adoption" as a bare label and rest on these rows. It is evident that the Lord sprang out of Juda because the line is registered in Joseph's house by Joseph's taking and naming, with no step needing Joseph's loins.

A second footing from Matthew's own line:

**[L1]** Matthew 1:11: "Josias begat Jechonias and his brethren". Matthew 1:12: "Jechonias begat Salathiel".

**[L3]** Jeremiah 22:24: "Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah". Jeremiah 24:1: "Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah". Jeremiah 22:30: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David". Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David".

**[L4]** Matthew's line to Joseph passes by "begat" through Jechonias, who is Jeconiah and Coniah, the son of Jehoiakim. Jeremiah 22:30 bars the seed of that man from the throne of David. Luke 1:32 gives Jesus that throne. A son of Joseph's loins would be Jechonias' seed by Matthew's own "begat" chain. A son who is Joseph's by taking and naming would not be. This is a further reason the throne comes by Joseph's house and not by Joseph's begetting.

**Hebrews 2:14-17.** The text says he took on him "the seed of Abraham" (Hebrews 2:16, [L1]). *Sperma* (G4690) is "seed (including the male 'sperm'); by implication, offspring". The verse states descent and does not name a father as the channel. Hebrews 2:17 says "in all things... made like unto [his] brethren". I accept that this includes real flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14). It does not say all things of his origin, since Hebrews 10:5 says "a body hast thou prepared me". Footings: Hebrews 2:16 [L1] with *sperma* [L2], Hebrews 10:5 [L3].

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 4, CLOSE ROUND

## CLOSE ROUND: final defense of D1 to D6

**Status of the chain.**
- D1, D2, D4 and D6 are KEPT.
- D3 is NARROWED TO: Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:25 for the limb "not known," with the [L2] for "virgin" taken from the verses where *parthenos* stands.
- D5 is NARROWED TO: Galatians 4:4 and Genesis 3:15 name the woman and no man, and I rest no exclusion of a father on them alone.
- Two things are conceded outright:
  - No quoted row states Mary's descent from David. None of D1 to D6 rests on it.
  - The Jeconiah step (Jeremiah 22:30) was never a declared link. I withdraw it (see the answers on 1 Chronicles 3:17 and Psalms 132:11).

---

### D1: the "begat" pattern breaks at Joseph

- [L1] Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob."
- [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L2] *ex hēs* (ἐξ ἧς) means "out of whom." The relative is feminine singular, so it cannot take Joseph as its antecedent. *gennaō* (G1080) is "properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother."
- [L4] Footed on Matthew 1:2 and Matthew 1:16, with *ex hēs*: the active "begat" runs to Joseph and stops. Joseph is named "the husband of Mary," not the one who begat Jesus. The birth is then assigned out of a feminine antecedent.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:16 -- D1 --** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- The challenger says the passive is "the mother's side" of *gennaō* and that the verse "joins husband, wife and birth."
- Granted. But a verse that wanted Joseph to be the begetter would repeat the pattern of Matthew 1:2, "begat."
- [L1] The verse instead gives Joseph a different title, "the husband of Mary," and puts the birth in the feminine "of whom."
- [L3] Luke 3:23 says the same of Joseph: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
- The mother's side of the verb is exactly what the text uses.

**ANSWER: Numbers 1:18 -- D1, D6 --** "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers, according to the number of the names."
- This verse is about how Israel was counted for the muster. It does not say that no child entered a house except by a father's begetting.
- [L3] The KJV itself records houses reckoned without begetting. Genesis 48:5: "Ephraim and Manasseh... [are] mine; as Reuben and Simeon, they shall be mine." Ruth 4:17: "There is a son born to Naomi."
- [L3] Luke 2:4 gives Joseph "the house and lineage of David."
- [L2] *patria* (G3965) there is "paternal descent," a group of families.
- [L4] Footed on Genesis 48:5 with Ruth 4:17 for reckoning into a house, and Luke 2:4 for Joseph's house: Joseph gives the house by reckoning, "as was supposed" (Luke 3:23). Numbers 1:18 is a rule of counting and does not make Joseph the begetter.

**ANSWER: Hebrews 7:14 -- D1 --** "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda."
- The verse says only that the Lord sprang out of Juda. It does not say through whom.
- Romans 1:3 fixes the sense: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- [L2] *sperma* (G4690) is "seed... offspring." *sarx* (G4561) is "flesh" as "the means of kindred."
- [L3] The KJV gives "seed" to women: Genesis 16:10, "I will multiply thy seed exceedingly," said to the woman Hagar. Genesis 3:15 says "her seed." Genesis 4:25 has Eve say "hath appointed me another seed."
- [L4] Footed on Romans 1:3 with *sperma*, and on Genesis 16:10 with Genesis 4:25: "seed" in the KJV is reckoned to a woman's offspring. So "seed of David according to the flesh" does not demand Joseph's loins.

**ANSWER: Acts 2:30 -- D1, D6 --** "that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."
- **ANSWER: 2 Samuel 7:12 -- D1, D6 --** "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels."
- **ANSWER: Psalms 132:11 -- D6 --** "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne." [body: Heb. belly]
- [L2] *mê'eh* (H4578) is "bowels." *'osphys* means "loins."
- Both name David's own body as the source of the line. Neither names an intermediate father.
- [L3] Luke 1:32 gives the throne as God's act: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."
- [L3] Hebrews 7:10 uses "in the loins of his father" of Abraham, who stands remote from Levi (Matthew 1:2). So "father" and "loins" in these rows name an ancestor.
- [L4] Footed on Psalms 132:11 with Acts 2:30, and on Luke 1:32 with Hebrews 7:10: the promise requires only David's descendant. It does not require Joseph as the begetter, and "his father David" is the language of ancestry.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:27 and Luke 2:4 -- D1 --**
- Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David."
- Luke 2:4: "because he was of the house and lineage of David."
- Conceded: the house of David is named on Joseph in both verses.
- [L2] *parthenos* (G3933) in Luke 1:27 is "a maiden... virgin." The same verse that names Joseph's house calls Mary "a virgin."
- [L3] Luke 3:23 gives Joseph's relation to the child as "as was supposed."
- [L4] Footed on Luke 1:27 with *parthenos*, and on Luke 2:4 with Luke 3:23: Joseph's house is the house the child is reckoned into. That is D4's point and does not touch D1.

---

### D2: the conception was of the Holy Ghost, before they came together

- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* means "out of the Spirit, holy."
- [L3] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:18 -- D2 --** "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- The challenger puts the knowing "within the espousal," before the finding.
- But the verse's own order is "before they came together" and then "found with child." The coming together is Joseph's taking of her, and Matthew 1:24 says "took unto him his wife."
- [L3] Matthew 1:19 shows what Joseph did when he found her: he "was minded to put her away privily."
- [L3] Matthew 1:20 gives the ground that removes his fear: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L4] Footed on Matthew 1:18 with Matthew 1:19-20: a man who knew himself to be the father would have no cause to put her away. And the angel's "for" would have no work to do if the conception were Joseph's. The conception is placed before the union and ascribed to the Holy Ghost.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:19 -- D2 --** "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
- Conceded: betrothal made her his wife in law (Deuteronomy 22:24, "his neighbour's wife"). *apolyō* (G630) is "divorce... put away."
- That law-status is not the knowing. The verse gives his state of mind. A just man, "not willing to make her a publick example" (*paradeigmatizō*, "make a public example"), would not meet a pregnancy he knew was his own with a thought of putting her away.
- [L4] Footed on Matthew 1:19 with *paradeigmatizō*, and on Deuteronomy 22:24: the verse shows the bond. It does not show knowing, and it counts against it.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:20 -- D2, D6 --** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." [conceived: Gr. begotten]
- The challenger sets "of God" with *gennaō* in 1 John 5:1 ("Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God") and John 1:13.
- [L3] John 1:13 itself reads: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
- There, "of God" is set against the will of man. [L2] *gennaō* is also "figuratively, to regenerate," and that is the sense in 1 John 5:1.
- In Matthew 1:20 the word is bodily: "conceived in her." The origin named is "of the Holy Ghost," and no man.
- [L4] Footed on John 1:13 with the *gennaō* gloss, and on Matthew 1:20 with its margin "Gr. begotten": the parallel shows "of God" standing where "of the will of man" is denied. The title "son of David" names Joseph's house, as Luke 2:4 does, and does not make him the source.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:24 -- D2 --** "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife."
- The taking comes after the finding, so the coming together is after the conception.
- [L3] Deuteronomy 20:7 ("hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her") separates betrothal from taking.
- [L4] Footed on Matthew 1:24 with Deuteronomy 20:7: the taking is after the child is already conceived (Matthew 1:18).

---

### D3 (NARROWED): virgin, and Joseph did not know her

- [L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- [L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- [L2] *ginōskō* (G1097) is "to know." *parthenos* (G3933) is "virgin," in Luke 1:27 and Matthew 1:23.
- [L3] Genesis 24:16 defines the KJV's word "virgin": "a virgin, neither had any man known her."
- Conceded: *parthenos* does not stand in Isaiah 7:14. I rest the "virgin" limb on Luke 1:27 and Matthew 1:23 with Genesis 24:16, not on Isaiah 7:14.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:34 -- D3 --** "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- The challenger says this is her present state, with the conceiving in the future (Luke 1:31, "thou shalt conceive in thy womb").
- That is exactly the question. "How shall this be" asks about the future conception, given a present state of not knowing a man.
- [L3] The answer in Luke 1:35 gives no man: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee."
- [L3] Compare Luke 1:13: to Zacharias, "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son." Zacharias is named as the one she bears to. Mary's answer names the Holy Ghost.
- [L4] Footed on Luke 1:34 with *ginōskō*, and on Luke 1:35: a question of "how," met by an answer that names no man.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:35 -- D2, D3 --** "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- The challenger sends the "therefore" back to Luke 1:32.
- But the "therefore" stands in the same verse, directly after "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee." The cause the verse names is that coming and that power.
- [L3] The challenger's Acts 1:8 ("after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you") and Luke 9:34 ("there came a cloud, and overshadowed them") show these verbs of power. They do not turn "come upon" into a husband's approach.
- [L4] Footed on Luke 1:35 with Luke 1:34: the verse names the Holy Ghost as the reason the child is called the Son of God, and names no man.

**ANSWER: Matthew 1:25 -- D3 --** "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- The challenger bounds the "not knowing" to the time after the taking.
- Granted, the verse follows the taking of Matthew 1:24. But Matthew 1:18 already has her "found with child" before they came together.
- [L4] Footed on Matthew 1:18 with Matthew 1:25: at the taking she was already with child, and he knew her not "till" the birth. Nothing in the rows gives a knowing before Matthew 1:18.

**ANSWER: Isaiah 8:3 -- D3 --** "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son." [went: Heb. approached]
- [L2] *qarab* (H7126) behind the margin is "come near."
- Isaiah 8:3 describes the prophet's own son, who is told to be named "Mahershalalhashbaz." Isaiah 7:14 says "shall call his name Immanuel."
- [L1] Matthew 1:22-23 states its own fulfilment: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child."
- [L3] Isaiah 7:11: "Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above."
- [L4] Footed on Matthew 1:22-23 with Isaiah 7:11: the text of Matthew claims the virgin's sign. A sign asked "in the depth, or in the height above," is not an ordinary conception. I do not rest on Isaiah 8:3 against the near child.

**ANSWER: Isaiah 7:14 -- D3 --** "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son." [shall call: or, thou, O virgin, shalt call]
- Conceded: *parthenos* is not in this verse. The Hebrew word here is *'almah* (H5959), printed "virgin" by the KJV.
- [L3] The KJV's own definition of "virgin" is Genesis 24:16: "neither had any man known her."
- [L3] Genesis 25:21 gives Rebekah "his wife" conceiving, a different case from a virgin conceiving.
- [L4] Footed on Genesis 24:16 with Matthew 1:23: the KJV's "virgin" means one who is unknown. Matthew 1:23 gives the word as *parthenos*, and the fulfilment of "a virgin shall be with child" is placed on Mary.

**ANSWER: Luke 1:36 and Luke 1:37 -- D3 --**
- Luke 1:36: "she hath also conceived a son in her old age... who was called barren."
- Luke 1:37: "For with God nothing shall be impossible."
- The "also" matches conceiving with conceiving (*syllambanō* G4815 in both Luke 1:31 and 1:36).
- It does not match the means. For Elisabeth the means is her husband, since Luke 1:13 says "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son." For Mary the means given in Luke 1:35 is the Holy Ghost.
- [L4] Footed on Luke 1:36 with Luke 1:13, and on Luke 1:35: the "for" in Luke 1:37 gives a general ground (nothing impossible with God). It does not turn Mary's case into Elisabeth's.

---

### D4: Joseph called father "as was supposed"

- [L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
- [L2] *enomizeto* (G3543) is "was supposed, was reckoned."
- [L3] Luke 4:22: "And they said, Is not this Joseph's son?" John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?"
- [L4] Footed on Luke 3:23 with *enomizeto*, and on Luke 4:22 and John 6:42: the people's "we know" is the supposition Luke 3:23 reports. Luke 2:48-49 sets Mary's "thy father and I" beside Jesus's reply, "my Father's business."

**ANSWER: Luke 1:62 and Matthew 1:21 -- D4 --** "they made signs to his father, how he would have him called," and "she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS."
- [L3] Genesis 4:25 says of Eve: "she bare a son, and called his name Seth."
- [L3] Luke 1:31 gives the naming to Mary: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS."
- So the naming is given to the mother as well. It does not prove begetting.
- [L1] The forms differ in the very verses the challenger sets side by side. Luke 1:13 says "bear thee a son." Matthew 1:21 says only "she shall bring forth a son."
- [L4] Footed on Genesis 4:25 with Luke 1:31, and on Luke 1:13 with Matthew 1:21: naming is given to both parents, and the angel's "bear thee" is dropped in Matthew 1:21.

---

### D5 (NARROWED): "made of a woman," the woman's seed

- [L1] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman."
- [L2] *genomenon ek gynaikos* means "come to be out of a woman."
- [L3] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed."
- Conceded: Galatians 4:4 and Genesis 3:15 name the woman and are silent about a father. Matthew 11:11, "born of women," is said of John, whose father is named in Luke 1:13. I do not claim these two verses exclude a father.
- [L3] The exclusion rests on Matthew 1:18, Matthew 1:20, Luke 1:34-35 and Matthew 1:25 (D2, D3, D6). Galatians 4:4 stands beside those rows without contradicting them.

**ANSWER: Galatians 4:4 and Romans 1:3 -- D5 --**
- Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- [L2] *ginomai* (G1096) is "to cause to be... be made." The challenger says it takes the seed-word as its source.
- Granted. But Genesis 16:10 and Genesis 4:25 give "seed" to the woman as well. The seed-word does not settle the route.
- [L4] Footed on Romans 1:3 with Genesis 16:10: the verse fixes David's descent and leaves the route to the other rows.

---

### D6: therefore no human biological father

- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." [conceived: Gr. begotten]
- [L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L2] *gennēthen* (G1080) is "conceived, begotten," and in the KJV margin "begotten." Its gloss is "properly, of the father." *ek pneumatos hagiou* is "out of the Spirit, holy."
- [L3] Luke 1:34: "seeing I know not a man." Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- [L4] Footed on Matthew 1:20 with the margin "begotten," and on Luke 1:34 with Matthew 1:25: the verb that properly belongs to the father's act is given with its source as the Holy Ghost. The rows name no man as the source, and they exclude the knowing before the birth.

**ANSWER: 1 Chronicles 3:17 -- D6 --** "And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son." [Salathiel: Heb. Shealtiel]
- Conceded: Jeconiah had a son, Salathiel. [L1] Matthew 1:12 says "Jechonias begat Salathiel."
- [L2] *zera'* (H2233) in Jeremiah 22:30 is "seed... posterity." The verse itself says "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David."
- The Jeconiah step was a supporting remark and never a declared link. D6 stands on D2 and D3 and does not need it. I withdraw it.

**ANSWER: Ezra 2:61 and Ezra 2:62 -- D1 --**
- Ezra 2:61: "which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name."
- Ezra 2:62: "therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood."
- The challenger takes this as a register refusing a line carried by the wife's house.
- But the verse says "These sought their register [among] those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found." This is about the priesthood register.
- [L3] Hebrews 7:14 says of Juda "Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood." The rule of Ezra 2:62 is a priestly rule.
- [L4] Footed on Ezra 2:62 with Hebrews 7:14: the case shows how a man took a wife's name in a priestly register. It does not show how flesh descends in a case where no begetting by a man is stated.

---

### Summary of the held ground

The challenger's whole case, that Joseph is the father, needs a knowing of Mary by Joseph before Matthew 1:18. No quoted row gives it. The rows that bear on the point say the opposite.
- Matthew 1:18 says "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- Matthew 1:20 says "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." [conceived: Gr. begotten]
- Luke 1:35 names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and no man.
- Matthew 1:25 says "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- Matthew 1:16 turns to the feminine "of whom."
- Luke 3:23 calls Joseph the father "as was supposed."

The challenger answers with the Davidic route, the register, and the parallels of Elisabeth and Isaiah 8:3. None of these quotes a row naming Joseph as the source of the child.

# Challenger's Answer: The Seed of David Came out of Joseph's Loins, and Joseph Was His Father

My position is that Christ had a biological father, Joseph of the house of David, husband of Mary. I aim at the defender's keystone, D6, and at the links it stands on: D1, D2, D3, D4 and D5.

---

## PRESS ON D6 (keystone): "Therefore Christ had no human biological father"

D6 stands on Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35. Read whole, both verses name the human house.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]" The same verse that says "of the Holy Ghost" names Joseph "son of David" and calls Mary "thy wife."

**[L2]** "Of" is *ek* ("out of, from"). The margin's "begotten" is *gennaō* (G1080, "to beget"). The same verb, with *ek* and God, is said of believers:

**[L3]** 1 John 5:1: "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him." John 1:13: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." 1 John 3:9: "Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin."

**[L4]** These believers have fathers in the flesh. Yet the text says they are "born... of God" and "begotten of him." So *ek* with God or the Spirit names an origin in God, and it stands beside a father in the flesh. Matthew 1:20 carries both in one verse: "of the Holy Ghost" and "Joseph, thou son of David... Mary thy wife." Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:20, [L2] *ek* and *gennaō*, [L3] 1 John 5:1 and John 1:13. D6's reading of "of the Holy Ghost" as replacing the father does not fit these rows.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Dio kai* ("therefore also") points back to Luke 1:32, not forward to a divine begetting of flesh. Luke 1:32 reads: "He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." The title and the throne are given before Mary asks "How shall this be" (Luke 1:34). *Klēthēsetai* means "shall be called."

**[L3]** The title is a covenant title, given to a son who had a father in the flesh. 1 Chronicles 28:6: "Solomon thy son, he shall build my house and my courts: for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father." 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son."

Every New Testament occasion of Psalm 2:7 ("Thou [art] my Son; this day have I begotten thee") is a raising, a priesthood or the covenant promise:
- the resurrection: Acts 13:33, "in that he hath raised up Jesus again; as it is also written in the second psalm, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee";
- the priesthood: Hebrews 5:5, "Christ glorified not himself to be made an high priest; but he that said unto him, Thou art my Son, to day have I begotten thee";
- the covenant formula beside it: Hebrews 1:5, "Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? And again, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son?"

# Challenger, Final Round: The Fruit of David's Loins Came by the Named Davidic Father

The defender has now conceded two things. First, no quoted row gives Mary of the house of David. Second, "made of a woman" sets no father aside. Each concession bears on the keystone, D6. The text requires the Christ to be "of the seed of David according to the flesh." Once Mary's descent is conceded, the rows name one Davidic man in that house, and he is Joseph. I answer the defender's second round point by point and then list the breaks.

---

## 1. The throne is tied to the loins, so taking and naming cannot carry it (D6)

**[L1]** Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne." Psalm 132:11: "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne. [body: Heb. belly]"

**[L2]** 2 Samuel 7:12 says "which shall proceed out of thy bowels." The Hebrew is *me'eh* (H4578), "the uterus (or of men, the seat of generation)." Romans 1:3 says "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." The Greek words are *sperma* (G4690), "seed (including the male 'sperm')," and *sarx* (G4561), "flesh... the means of kindred."

**[L3]** Hebrews 7:10: "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him." Seed in the loins passes from father to son down the generations. Luke 2:4: "because he was of the house and lineage of David." The word for "lineage" is *patria* (G3965), "paternal descent."

**[L4]** In each of these promises the throne goes to the fruit of David's body or loins, "according to the flesh." The defender rests the throne on taking and naming. That gives the child a name in Joseph's house. It does not give him "the fruit of his loins." The defender has conceded Mary's descent. So the one channel of David's paternal descent the rows name is Joseph, who is "of the house and lineage (*patria*, paternal descent) of David." Footing: [L1] Acts 2:30 and Psalm 132:11; [L2] *me'eh*, *sperma* and *patria*; [L3] Hebrews 7:10 and Luke 2:4.

**The defender's own witnesses show the same thing.**
- **Genesis 48:5.** It speaks of "thy two sons... which were born unto thee." Ephraim and Manasseh were already of Jacob's loins through his son Joseph.
- **Ruth 4.** Ruth 4:13 says Boaz "went in unto her, the LORD gave her conception, and she bare a son." Ruth 4:21 says "Boaz begat Obed." The LORD's giving of conception stands with a husband's act.
- **Ezra 2:61-62.** The man who "was called after their name" ended this way: "therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood." This is the defender's own example of being registered by a name from another house, and the register refused it.

## 2. The curse does not move the throne off the loins (D6)

**[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30: "Write ye this man childless." Yet Matthew 1:12 says "Jechonias begat Salathiel," and 1 Chronicles 3:17 says "the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son, [Salathiel: Heb. Shealtiel]."

**[L3]** Jeremiah 22:24 plucks the signet: "yet would I pluck thee thence." Haggai 2:23 gives the signet back to Jeconiah's grandson: "O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel... will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee." Jeremiah 18:8 states the LORD's own rule for a sentence he has pronounced: "If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them."

**[L4]** The man written "childless" begat Salathiel. The signet that was plucked was set again on his line. Acts 2:30 still joins the throne to "the fruit of his loins." The defender uses the curse to cut the throne off from begetting. Haggai 2:23 and Acts 2:30, read together, do not allow that cut. Footing: [L1] Jeremiah 22:30 with Matthew 1:12; [L3] Haggai 2:23, Jeremiah 18:8 and Acts 2:30.

## 3. "Fear not" names the taking, and the same angel says "fear not" to a begetting father (D6)

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"

**[L2]** The thing Joseph is told not to fear is *paralambanō* (G3880), "to receive near... in any familiar or intimate act or relation." The fear is attached to taking her. The word for "wife" is *gynē* (G1135), "specially, a wife."

**[L3]** The angel speaks the same way to a father who begat his son. Luke 1:13: "Fear not, Zacharias: for thy prayer is heard; and thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son." The preposition *ek* with God also stands beside fathers in the flesh. John 1:13: "born... of God." 1 John 5:1: "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him."

**[L4]** "Fear not" followed by "for" grounds a command. In Luke 1:13 it grounds a father's own begetting. So the defender's step does not hold: "If Joseph's own act were the source, there would be nothing to fear." The defender also argues that the believers' "of God" in John 1:13 is a second birth. That point grants what I pressed. *Ek* with God names an origin in God, and it stands beside a father in the flesh. Matthew 1:20 joins both in one verse: "of the Holy Ghost" and "thou son of David... Mary thy wife." Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:20; [L2] *paralambanō* and *gynē*; [L3] Luke 1:13 and 1 John 5:1.

## 4. The angel's own example of the impossible is a wife conceiving by her husband (D2, D6)

**[L1]** Luke 1:36-37: "thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age: and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren. For with God nothing shall be impossible."

**[L2]** "Conceived" in Luke 1:36 is *syllambanō* (G4815), "specially, to conceive." It is the same verb as Mary's "thou shalt conceive" in Luke 1:31. *Kai* ("also") sets the two conceptions side by side. In Luke 1:35, *dio kai* ("therefore also") connects back to Luke 1:32 and not forward to a divine begetting of flesh. Luke 1:32 already gives "shall be called the Son of the Highest" and "the throne of his father David," and it comes before Mary asks "How shall this be" in Luke 1:34.

**[L3]** Elisabeth's conception came by her husband: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son" (Luke 1:13). The title fits a son who has a father in the flesh: "Solomon thy son... I have chosen him [to be] my son" (1 Chronicles 28:6).

**[L4]** The defender says Luke 1:37 "would have nothing to meet" if a husband were the means. The angel's own instance of "nothing shall be impossible" is a barren wife who conceived by her husband. So Luke 1:37 meets God's power working through a marriage. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:36-37; [L2] *syllambanō* and *dio kai*; [L3] Luke 1:13 and 1 Chronicles 28:6.

## 5. Mary's question and the timing rows (D3)

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb."

**[L2]** *Ginōskō* ("know") is in the present tense here, so it gives her condition when she spoke. The conceiving is future. *Anēr* (G435), "husband, man," is also the word for Joseph as "the husband of Mary" in Matthew 1:16.

**[L3]** Matthew 1:18 says "before they came together, she was found with child." That dates when she was found. Matthew 1:24-25 reads: "took unto him his wife: And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." The abstinence comes after the taking and is bounded by "till." In the law the betrothed woman is already "his neighbour's wife" (Deuteronomy 22:24). The canon's way of conceiving is knowing: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1).

**[L4]** Joseph was "her husband" (Matthew 1:19) from the espousal. The seed rows require the fruit of a Davidic man's loins. So Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins. Luke 1:34 is her state before the conception. Matthew 1:25 is the time after the taking. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:24-25; [L2] *ginōskō* and *anēr*; [L3] Genesis 4:1 and Deuteronomy 22:24.

**On Isaiah 7:14.**
- **[L1]** Isaiah 7:16 bounds the sign: "before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings."
- **[L3]** Isaiah 8:3-4 fulfils it in the same form: "I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son... [went: Heb. approached]... For before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother." Isaiah 8:8 addresses "thy land, O Immanuel" in that very invasion. Isaiah counts his children as the signs: "the children whom the LORD hath given me" are "for signs and for wonders in Israel" (Isaiah 8:18).
- **[L4]** The sign came by a husband's approach. Matthew 1:22-23 applies it, and the application keeps that shape.

## 6. Joseph's mind and Mary's "thy father" (D4)

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L2]** The verbs in this verse are *thelō* (G2309, "to determine... choose") and *boulomai* (G1014, "be willing"). Matthew 1:20 adds *enthymeomai* (G1760, "ponder"). The defender writes, "No verb of knowing is needed." That grants my point: the verse states his will and his pondering.

**[L3]** Mary heard the angel. She says "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48). Luke's own narration says "the parents brought in the child Jesus" (Luke 2:27). Luke 2:49's "my Father's business" stands beside Luke 2:48 as the two sonships of 1 Chronicles 28:6 stand together: "Solomon thy son" and "my son" in one verse.
